rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The mockery repeatedly intensified their arrogance until their jest effectively mocked God, while distracting them from His watching and coming requital.
rows.anchor: such was the extent of their jest and mockery that they did not get the time to think

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They should realize God watches their wrongdoing against His patient, grateful servants and will avenge every misdeed.
rows.anchor: God was fully watching their misdeeds with His patient and grateful servants; one day, He will definitely take revenge

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing statement calls the mockers to face the reality they had ignored: the persecuted servants who persevered are now rewarded and truly successful.
rows.anchor: Today they shall be fully rewarded for their perseverance and it is they who shall achieve really success.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah closes where it began, with the success of believers humble in prayer; this return to the beginning is a prominent sign of Qur'anic coherence.
rows.anchor: It is ending on the same note with which it began. This style of ‘awd ‘al ā al-bad’

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: These words of affection must have comforted and strengthened poor Muslims suffering persecution at the time.
rows.anchor: How much they must have been comforted and strengthened at these words of affection by their honourable God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The delay in resurrection will soon be exposed as a misconception: what people imagined to be a long earthly life will end like a blink.
rows.anchor: the life they thought was a long one would end in the blink of an eye.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening question's qala is not spoken by God or an angel; it means that some speaker will ask.
rows.anchor: The word ﻗٰﻞَ will not be uttered by God or by an angel

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The words qala are understood in the sense qala qail, meaning that a speaker will speak.
rows.anchor: It is actually in the sense of ﻗﺎل ﻗﺎﺋﻞa speaker will speak).

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The respondents' direction to ask those who counted expresses their aversion to a question about the life whose imagined length had enamored them.
rows.anchor: The words “but you ask this to those who have kept count” actually express aversion of the responders.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Someone among the respondents says earthly life was brief, with rebuke and regret that understanding came too late.
rows.anchor: The words “You only stayed for a short while. Would that you knew” will also be spoken from someone among them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: They lived in the world only briefly, but the chance to understand that truth has already passed.
rows.anchor: they stayed in the world for a short while but the time for this comprehension has now passed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dialogue about earthly life occurs among the people themselves, as the parallel exchange in Ṭāhā makes explicit.
rows.anchor: They will whisper to one another:

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The dialogue in the Cave sūrah likewise shows people speaking among themselves; it exemplifies awakening from sleep in Barzakh.
rows.anchor: There a dialogue is cited between the companions of the cave.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: People assume they will keep living only while alive; after life passes, it becomes a dream of the past.
rows.anchor: It is a fact that it is only as long as a person is living that he thinks that he will keep living.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: It is utterly mistaken to think that people were created without purpose, will not return to their Lord, and will not answer for their deeds.
rows.anchor: very wrong is their notion that they will not be returned to their Lord and not be held accountable

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's attributes answer idolaters' doubts about judgment: a real sovereign does not create pointlessly and must distinguish oppressor from oppressed.
rows.anchor: Since He is the real sovereign, how can it be possible that He does not administer justice between His servants

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The throne signifies God's governance, while glorious signifies His honour and benevolence; such a ruler's governance cannot be purposeless.
rows.anchor: The word “throne” signifies God’s governance and the word “glorious” signifies His honour and benevolence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Because no other deity exists, no one should imagine that intercession can save them from God’s grasp.
rows.anchor: no one should mislead himself by thinking that he can save himself from God’s grasp through any intercession.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah's ending contrasts its opening: believers are declared successful at the start, while disbelievers are said never to succeed at the end.
rows.anchor: The sūrah began with the words “Those believers succeeded who …” and is ending on the words “the disbelievers shall never succeed.”

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The companions are urged through the Prophet to ask God for forgiveness and mercy, continuing the prayer already mentioned in verse 109 and mocked by disbelievers.
rows.anchor: it is the same prayer which is referred to in verse 109 and which was made fun of by the disbelievers.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is to keep his stance and persist in the prescribed prayer, which will open forgiveness and mercy for him.
rows.anchor: the Prophet (sws) was to adhere to his stance and keep praying as told. It would open the doors of forgiveness and mercy for him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prayer also conveys glad tidings of victory and God's help for the believers.
rows.anchor: It is a glad tiding of victory

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Nūr has no counterpart because it supplements and appends al-Mu'minūn; such a supplement is effectively part of its preceding sūrah.
rows.anchor: a sūrah which is a supplement and appendix to the previous one is in fact a part of it

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Mu'minūn's opening describes success through humble prayer, avoiding frivolity, zakāh, chastity and restraint, trustworthiness, and keeping promises.
rows.anchor: salvation and success before God is reserved for those believers whose prayers are marked with humility and concentration

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In Mecca faith's consequences appeared mainly in individual lives; after migration and a collective political order in Medina, those consequences could shape communal life.
rows.anchor: time was ripe that these consequences of faith also find expression

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: As circumstances permitted, directives for communal reform and purification were revealed, extending the radiance of faith from individuals to society.
rows.anchor: this radiance of faith that was hitherto confined to their individual lives now extended to their collective lives also.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Nūr gives directives suited to its historical circumstances to correct the community's collective affairs and protect it from consequences contrary to faith.
rows.anchor: directives which can set right the collective affairs of their society and which were necessary to protect them

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening three verses address the punishment of fornication and prohibit a Muslim's marriage to an idolater or a person guilty of fornication.
rows.anchor: The punishment of fornication is mentioned, and the prohibition for a Muslim to marry an idolater

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 4–5 set out the punishment for accusing someone of fornication and the evidentiary rule for proving it.
rows.anchor: The punishment of accusing someone of fornication and the law of evidence related to prove this crime

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 6–10 resolve a husband's unsupported adultery accusation against his wife through a prescribed oath procedure.
rows.anchor: If a person accuses his wife of adultery and is not able to present the

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 11–26 expose hypocrites' role in the ifk scandal and give corrective warnings; negligent Muslims are cautioned, and accusations must not be believed without solid proof.
rows.anchor: Muslims who showed carelessness and negligence in this matter and thereby inadvertently strengthened the propaganda worked by the hypocrites are also warned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 27–31 regulate visiting other Muslims' homes and seeing those inside, while explaining restrictions for women present there.
rows.anchor: they must abide by certain decorum so that the eyes are restrained from taking undue liberty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 32–34 promote social purity through marriage for widows, widowers, and enslaved people, mukātabah and financial help toward it, and a ban on forcing slave women into prostitution.
rows.anchor: It is stressed upon Muslims to financially help slave-men and slave-women who want to undertake mukātabat.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The parable contrasts believers, whose hearts shine inwardly and outwardly, with unbelievers, surrounded by darkness.
rows.anchor: hearts which have faith in them shine both inwardly and outwardly.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Signs in the world show that God alone controls the universe and that all creation glorifies Him; humans therefore owe Him faith and exclusive worship.
rows.anchor: Only God, the one and only, is controlling this universe. Everything is glorifying and praising Him alone.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Opponents accept the Prophet when it serves them but otherwise disregard God and His messenger; true success requires committed obedience, not divided loyalties or false oaths.
rows.anchor: Opponents of the Prophet (sws) would agree with him if something was in their interest

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's responsibility to convey God's religion is complete; each person must now reflect on the consequences of their choice.
rows.anchor: His responsibility is to convey God’s religion which he has done. It is now left to people and each of them must contemplate his fate.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The righteous companions receive a clear promise of political authority, protection for their religion, and a change from fear to security, alongside duties of prayer, zakāh, and obedience to the Prophet.
rows.anchor: Soon the time will come when God will replace the current state of fear with peace and security.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 58–61 answer questions that arose about the gender-interaction instructions in verses 27–31; these verses were revealed after those questions were answered.
rows.anchor: Earlier in verses 27-31, directives related to gender interaction were given. Later some questions arose about them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The conclusion returns to obedience to the Prophet from verse 57: when he calls for communal work, Muslims, especially hypocrites, must respond and not leave without permission; their success depends on obedience.
rows.anchor: After the elucidatory verses, the discourse returns to the topic of obedience to the Prophet (sws) mentioned earlier in verse 57.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fornication destroys the purity of blood relations and sexual order, turning society into a herd of animals.
rows.anchor: The consequence of this is that a society is converted into a herd of animals.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The opening warns that a divinely revealed sūrah must not be treated as trivial; its commands must be obeyed.
rows.anchor: not regard it to be something trivial.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The declaration that its directives are mandatory means they must be followed without hesitation or negligence.
rows.anchor: They must be followed without any hesitancy and negligence in any way.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah intersperses admonitions at verses 1, 15, 17, 20, 24, 46, and 58, warning that directives must be observed in letter and spirit or God's punishment is stern.
rows.anchor: verses 1, 15, 17, 20, 24, 46 and 58 can be looked up.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Repeated warnings are a divine favor because family, social, and criminal rules had been pitfalls for earlier nations, and the warnings keep this community alert.
rows.anchor: It is a favour of God on this ummah that He besides giving these directives, He has also repeatedly informed it about the consequences

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Fornication disrupts lineage purity and social stability; because it roots disorder in society, all divine religions treat it as a punishable offense.
rows.anchor: all divine religions regard fornication to be a punishable offence.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Islam's initial rules in al-Nisāʾ 4:15–16 preceded circumstances suitable for punishment and anticipated a later, final directive, fulfilled here by one hundred lashes.
rows.anchor: initial directives given in this regard

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the clause about belief in God and the Last Day, the word dīn refers to the punishment for fornication stated here.
rows.anchor: The word دﻳۡﻦ in   ﻛ'ﻨۡﺘ'ﻢۡ ﺗ'ﺆۡﻣﻨ'ﻮۡنَ

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Faith requires applying the prescribed punishment without favoring rich over poor or showing softness to either sex; weakness here calls professed belief into question.
rows.anchor: no lenience should be shown in the implementation of this punishment; softness should be shown to neither

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The woman is mentioned before the man because fornication requires her consent and compassion may arise for her as the physically weaker party; the order signals equal enforcement.
rows.anchor: mentioned her before the man so that it becomes evident

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author says Jews had abandoned most prescribed punishments: their law prescribed stoning for fornication, but it was applied to the poor while the rich were spared.
rows.anchor: The punishment of fornication in their sharī‘ah was stoning to death but in reality it was only given to the poor

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He criticizes the modern view that criminals are mentally ill and should be rehabilitated rather than punished, arguing that lenience enables violent offenders.
rows.anchor: people who perpetrate crimes are mentally sick; thus they deserve to be sympathized with and rehabilitated instead of being punished.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He says contemporary lawmakers would call the prescribed penalty barbaric despite religious claims, while showing sympathy for offenders and neglecting murder, rape, and theft victims.
rows.anchor: no emotions of concern and sympathy arise in them for those who are murdered, raped or looted in large numbers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He argues the fear of prescribed punishments deters theft and fornication in Saudi Arabia, based on his own observations and eyewitness accounts, while acknowledging he lacks statistics.
rows.anchor: I do not have these statistics but I have heard what eye-witnesses say in this regard and at the same time what I myself have observed

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He sees an absurd reversal in the sympathy for offenders: people act as if they are more merciful to them than the Most Merciful God.
rows.anchor: it is as if they have become more merciful to them than the Most Merciful God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Public punishment makes offenders exemplary and teaches observers; the cited term means exemplary punishment, a purpose lost if penalties are administered in jail.
rows.anchor: to make them exemplary these punishments must be given in public. If they are administered in jails, this purpose is lost.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects some exegetes' claim that the required group of witnesses can mean a single person, questioning the basis of that interpretation.
rows.anchor: Some exegetes think that the word “group” also applies to a single individual.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although the verse's apparent wording covers all men and women guilty of fornication, jurists propose specifications; he considers some correct, others wrong, and some needing elaboration.
rows.anchor: all types of men and women guilty of fornication are included in it. However, our jurists have imposed certain specifications

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The punishment is enforceable only by an Islamic state, and the directives came after such a state was established in Medina.
rows.anchor: this punishment can only be implemented in an Islamic state.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Only mature adults are subject to the punishment; juveniles and people with lunacy are exempt, a premise he calls self-evident.
rows.anchor: Juveniles and those inflicted with lunacy are exempt from it.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Enslaved men and women receive half the punishment, based on al-Nisāʾ 4:25; gradual reform addressed their degraded social conditions, and later mukātabah enabled able-minded slaves' emancipation and equal rights.
rows.anchor: slave-men and slave-women will only be administered half of this punishment.

rows.speaker: one group of our jurists
rows.claim: One jurist group exempts non-Muslim subjects from this punishment, treating their personal affairs as outside public laws.
rows.anchor: Fourthly, one group of our jurists say that this punishment will only be implemented on Muslims.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects exempting non-Muslims from crimes whose punishments preserve public peace and justice: unequal treatment would license the offense and contradict the Prophet's and caliphs' practice.
rows.anchor: how can it be possible to sustain this exemption in punishments

rows.speaker: almost all jurists
rows.claim: Almost all jurists restrict the hundred lashes to unmarried offenders or marriages not consummated; a consummated married offender receives stoning, based on the Prophet's and caliphs' practice, which they treat as Sunnah abrogating the verse's rule for them.
rows.anchor: almost all jurists are of the view that this punishment only relates to criminals who are unmarried

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He is dissatisfied with specifying or abrogating a Qur'anic rule through a solitary report; the Kharijites likewise reject this method and deny stoning, applying the verse to all offenders.
rows.anchor: one is not satisfied to see a directive

rows.speaker: the khawārij
rows.claim: The Kharijites reject specifying or abrogating the verse this way, deny stoning, and apply the stated punishment to every offender.
rows.anchor: Thus the khawārij do not accept specifying or abrogating this directive in such a manner.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He distinguishes newer Kharijites, who reject flogging as well as stoning, and says the Qur'anic source and scope of stoning must be explained.
rows.anchor: The new ones are not even willing to accept flogging, let alone stoning.

rows.speaker: ‘Ubādah ibn Ṣāmit
rows.claim: Ubādah reports the Prophet saying that unmarried offenders receive one hundred lashes and a year in exile, while married offenders receive lashes and stoning.
rows.anchor: The following narrative reported by ‘Ubā dah ibn Ṣāmit is the one on the basis of which our jurists

rows.speaker: Hanafite and Shafite jurists
rows.claim: They say flogging and stoning are not combined; the verse's flogging rule was abrogated by the Prophet's and companions' practice, leaving stoning alone for married offenders.
rows.anchor: The Hanafite and Shafite jurists say that lashes and stoning cannot be given together

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He rejects abrogating the verse through the Ubādah report, since only the Qur'an can abrogate the Qur'an; he says the report actually accords with it and entails no abrogation.
rows.anchor: nothing except the Qur’ ān can abrogate the Qur’ān.

rows.speaker: Ibn ‘Abbās
rows.claim: Ibn ‘Abbās transmits ʿUmar's fear that people would deny a stoning verse and be led astray; ʿUmar says they once recited a command to stone married adulterers.
rows.anchor: Ibn ‘Abbās stated: “ ‘Umar ibn al-Kha ṭṭāb said: ‘I fear that time will pass over people

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He cites the report about a lost stoning verse reluctantly to answer doubts, and says its appearance suggests fabrication by a hypocrite to undermine confidence in Qur'anic preservation.
rows.anchor: Deliberation on this narrative shows that it seems to have been fabricated in every way by a hypocrite

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: He questions whether anyone upright could regard the wording attributed as a Qur'anic verse.
rows.anchor: Let us first reflect on the language of the narrative.
